football_evidence.question: Can Oregon get Northwestern off the field on third down?
football_evidence.assessment: Some measured evidence supports EdgeDesk’s lean toward Northwestern, and its own breakdown accounts for about 0.6 of the 5.3 points, but not the full gap. Input warning: EdgeDesk’s published number sits 12.8 points from the middle of its own other models. It is a research question, not a bet.
supporting: When Northwestern has the ball (big plays through the air): Northwestern’s offense turns 13.9% of its pass plays into explosive gains, and Oregon’s defense gives up explosive gains on 10.3% of opponent pass plays (FBS average 10.3%).

When Northwestern has the ball (big plays on the ground): Northwestern’s offense turns 10.1% of its runs into explosive gains, and Oregon’s defense gives up explosive gains on 6.0% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.5%).

When Oregon has the ball (the passing game against the pass defense): Oregon’s offense averages 6.6 yards per pass attempt, and Northwestern’s defense allows 6.1 yards per pass attempt (FBS average 7.4).
When Oregon has the ball (the red zone): Oregon’s offense succeeds on 45.9% of its red-zone plays, and Northwestern’s defense allows success on 31.8% of opponent red-zone plays (FBS average 43.6%).
contradicting: When Northwestern has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Northwestern’s offense has allowed a sack on 8.9% of its dropbacks, and Oregon’s defense sacks the quarterback on 7.2% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.7%).

When Oregon has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Oregon’s offense has allowed a sack on 3.5% of its dropbacks, and Northwestern’s defense sacks the quarterback on 6.3% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.7%).
